newsitem.title: USA: Dole heads west on second night of marathon.
newsitem.headline: Dole heads west on second night of marathon.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole on Saturday headed westward into the second night of round-the-clock campaigning that he hopes will turn his narrowing poll gap into an election victory.
"There is something happening across America ... I think we're going to win this race," a still-fired-up Dole said at the day's seventh campaign appearance in as many states.
Dole was then to head for South Dakota, Colorado and Las Vegas, Nevada, for late-night rallies before arriving in California before dawn.
Dole was in the second day of a non-stop campaign marathon that began on Friday and was to continue until he casts his vote in his hometown of Russell, Kansas, on Tuesday.

By late afternoon, Dole's face had begun to look slightly drawn, and his voice slowed. But he bounced back at the evening rally in a hangar at the Omaha airport, with a stem-winder of a stump speech dotted with wisecracks and concluded with a flourish as he tossed campaign hats to the crowd.
On Saturday, Dole fired away at alleged campaign-finance improprieties and ethical lapses of President Bill Clinton's administration, while taking heart at polls that showed him gaining on Clinton.

"We've had literally a scandal a week in this administration the past several weeks. I think the American people are starting to say 'what's going on there? What's going on in this White House?'" he said at a rally in Indianapolis.
Dole is lagging Clinton in the polls ahead of Tuesday's election but hopes his marathon tactics will inject enthusiasm into his campaign and swing voters to his side.

In the Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll released on Saturday, Dole had closed the gap between him and Clinton to 3.8 percentage points -- 42.4 percent to 38.6 percent, with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot at 8.4 percent. Other polls, however, show Clinton with a much larger margin.
Commenting on new polls, Dole told reporters on his plane, "I think it's moving in our direction."
"I think it's tightening up everywhere. A lot of good numbers floating around. A lot of polls out tomorrow," he said.

A senior adviser to Dole, Charlie Black, told reporters the campaign's own polls, which ended on Thursday, showed Dole gaining rapidly. "Our last poll had us closing three points a day, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday."
The poll on Thursday, assuming an optimistic turnout rate of 70 percent, showed Dole 6 percentage points behind Clinton.
Dole said he intended to finish his campaign in Independence, Missouri, the hometown of Harry Truman -- a Democrat -- who came from behind to win the 1948 presidential race.
"We're going to do it again ... a second Harry Truman," Dole said. "We're going to make it happen."
Dole told the Indianapolis rally that if Clinton were re- elected his ability to lead would be crippled by investigations into alleged improprieties.
"If he's re-elected he's going to spend half of his time next year with investigations ... who knows what will happen in the next 24 months, 36 months," Dole said.

On Saturday, he added new stops to his itinerary, bringing to 19 the number of states on his route. He was to campaign all day on Sunday in California, then on Monday he goes to Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee and Iowa.
"Ninety-six hours. Non stop. Non stop. Non stop. Non stop. Non stop," Dole said at a breakfast in Philadelphia on Saturday.
Dole spoke then about the disorienting effects of the campaign endurance race. "I can't remember when we started, but I can remember where we've been," he said.
Dole told reporters around midday he had taken some naps on the plane, bringing his total sleeping time to about 2 1/2 hours since Friday morning.
He said earlier he felt a "little bit" tired. "Not bad, though," he said. "We'll be all right. I'm starting to get used to it."
When he was asked how he felt after the Omaha rally, Dole said, "I feel great!"
